Army on Cape Flats - is it sustainable?

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
is the Army making a dent?

Unique Selling Point:
On patrol with the army. The real reason why the `Police are not able to contain the violence.

Summary:
Two weeks ago we told the story of the despair gripping the Western CAPE, following the execution of 6 young women……and on the weekend of our broadcast there were another 52 killings in the western cape. We ended off the program telling viewers that it was decided to bring in the army, and we highlighted concerns that this may escalate the violence.

Two weeks later, there has been a dramatic decrease in the numbers of murders. I have lots of footage of the army in the townships. And it shows the effect of boots on the ground. It is having am deterrent effect as the army support the police in their operations. The question is – how long can this be maintained since its costing R25 million for the first three months of deployment? Also there have been no incidents yet of untoward behavior from the troops.



Further information:
Regarding the deployment of the troops, we will speak to gangsters and ask them their thoughts….. and we will ask residents on the streets for their opinion.

We must never forget why the army have been called in. We speak to top Professor Nicol who runs trauma at Groot Schuur. A wonderful man, he talks about how they seldom see victims with single shot wounds. It’s now multiple. He is treating one woman with 20 bullet wounds. We will be allowed to speak to patients recovering in hospital, to hear their stories, and we will also hear how the hospital has developed a procedure from the army – its called shunting. To save multi would victims from dying from loss of blood, they stabilize the patient by inserting plastic into arteries. I have a video of such a procedure.

Here is the context of the story. We understand long term solutions are required but in the mean time the SA police have failed dismally in crime prevention and the reason is not hard to figure out. The lack of police in the Western Cape. The United Nations acceptable police per capita stands at 1 : 250. In Cape Town its 1: 600. In some gangster infested areas like Bonteheuwel on the Cape Flats its 1: 10 000.

This brings us to another element of the story. Crime fighting in the The Western Cape is not the mandate of the City of Cape Town. Yet they have trained up 100’s of law enforcement officers to deploy into areas. They have flooded Bonteheuwal since the first of this month with 100 officers– as a result of this deployment, there had not been a single murder reported in this Cape Flats area. We go on patrol with them. They will be here for 5 years. The City understands that it does not have the budget to create more law enforcement officers which is required to stem the tide But we are seeing results from extra boots on the ground – the city’s deployment in Bonteheuwal, and the army on the cape flats.

This leads up to the next section – the Western Cape Govt is planning to take the Nat Minister of Police to court – and attempting to get a court to force the Nat Govt to fill, the vacant 4500 police posts in the western cape. The above will be woven into the story.

To interview- gangsters, Prof Nicol, Patients, vox pops from people on the street for and against the army, the WC Commissioner of Police who can details the police’s action plan. The head of the Unit of City of Cape Town squad in Bonteheuwal as they go on patrol. Perhaps a defense force security expert who can talk about how cash strapped the army is, and how it is unfeasible for them to remain for a great length of time on the Cape Flats. And the W Cape premier who wants to take the Govt to court.

As we spend two days on the go, from following the army from its base to their next target, we will pick up extra reality style interviews

Script:


VO: It’s a week-day afternoon in tafellsig western Western Cape. Slowly meandering between homes, with kids playing on the streets, , are armoured vehicles from the South African National Defence force.


VO: For human rights activist Roegchanda Pascoe, the army’s arrival is not one moment too soon. This house where she has to stay, for now, is a safehouse to protect her and her family from reprisal by gangsters against whom she testified in court.


Pascoe: for me the army was like brining that stability because I knew the tiredness of our people, I knew they could not handle anymore.

VO: Carte Blanche was here just after the deadly weekend of 6 and 7 July, when 11 people were murdered in Phillipi east.. Six of the deceased were young women who were shot dead execution-style. That was the weekend that tipped the scales. Before then, Minister Bheki Cele had rejected calls for the army to step in. But after that weekend, he made a surprise announcement in Parliament.

Cele: (Parliament footage): we are deploying the army

LINK: 1200 troops were flown into Cape Town and they started their patrolling in designated areas of the Cape Flats.

VO> The army arrived 3 weeks ago and it was a few days before they were seen on the streets. Their modus operando seems to be to support the police hunting for wanted gangsters, drugs and illegal firearms.

As we followed them, residents appeared to welcome their presence.


VO: But Yusuf, a reformed gangster who asked to remain anonymous, has his doubts.

REFORMED GANGSTER: it does have a little impact but its like a pinch. The army is here now, but everybody is afraid…as soon as the army leaves everything will go back to normal.

VO: The troop deployment is reported to be costing the cash-strapped SANDF R23 million for the first three months. Eldred de Klerk specialises in comparative policing and social conflict and he feels that the army can maintain its presence.

De Klerk: They have a reserve budget for this kind of thing from which they will take this money to allow themselves to go and excerise this duty – but they have supplementary budgets with other departments that will have to pay back some of the money spend to pay back the army.

VO: After the first week, the army’s deployment led to a drop in the weekend murder rate from 42 to 25. But that was short-lived – the next weekend 46 people were killed. Observers attributed the spike to payday when crime stats are generally higher.

VO: It was the trauma team at the specialist referral hospital Groote Schuur that picked up the pieces after the mayhem.

LINK: It is mind boggling to understand how doctors cope in the trauma units. I walked through the GS hospital and have counted at least 30 patients that are in need to serious medical attention from gun shot wounds to stabbing wounds

VO: For the last 20 years, Professor Andrew Nicol has led the trauma team. They treat more than 70 gunshot victims every month – they have been deeply disturbed by the severity of injuries they see lately.

NICOLS: Instead of a person being shot once, we seem them coming in being shot multiple times..we admitted a patient 2 weeks ago who had 37 holes in her body.

VO: Nicol and his team use ground-breaking procedures developed by the military. This young man was shot 6 times and was bleeding to death. Repairing a partially severed femoral artery caused by a bullet would normally take too long. A quick fix was needed.

NICOLS: So what we do is place a piece of drip set into the artery to reestablish blood flow, and to stop the bleeding. It’s a rapid intervention but it allows them to survive this type of injury and to keep his leg

VO: This young man and countless other victims from the Cape Flats owe their lives to the quick and innovative treatment at Groot Schuur.

NICOL: its quite staggering what we can get through with patients there days using these types of techniques and currently two thirds are surviving by this type of abbreviated surgery.

VO: Back in the community, it’s mothers like Roegshanda Pacoe who have to find a way to fight back against the deadly gangs every day. Three years ago she witnessed a horrific gang fight in front of her home in Mannanberg.

Pascoe: People were standing in their windows and their doors and they were watching and screaming...myself as well, we could not intervene, there were too much.

VO: Angelo Davids was brutally killed that day. Roegshanda tried to help him, but there was little she could do as she faced his killers – she remains haunted by their eyes.

Pacoe: THE Coldness, the way nothing was going to change their minds only by the mission they are here to do…and execute….it is the worst I have ever seen.

VO: When no one on her street was prepared to come forward as a witness Roegshanda made a life-changing decision and took her children into her confidence.

Pascoe: I will never be able to live with myself knowing that I have seen and knowing that I have done nothing. I am going to testify, but I know it is going to impact on your lives.

VO: The price has been high. On the day before she testified Roegshanda’s home was shot at by gangsters. She wasn’t at home – her children called her in desperation.

Pascoe: I could hear the screams of my grand children, hear them saying – ma ma please come and help us..they going to kill us, and the fear that momement to be away from my children was the worst ever.

VO: Despite the family's terrifying ordeal, Roegshanda did testify in court. The family are now in a safe house and she remains in touch with other activists about the army’s deployment.

Pascoe: They are the police security now..but not the people or the community at large.

VO: Her feelings are echoed by more residents who feel that patrolling in an area for a short time and then moving on has little lasting effect.

VO: Minister Cele since has promised another 1000 police officers for the Western Cape.

VO: But Western Cape Premier Alan Winde says it’s not enough – he is asking for 4500 extra police. He’s launched an intergovernmental dispute on policing and is prepared to go to court to get those extra officers – because it all boils down to ratios, he says.

Allan Winde: So the SA ratio, one officer to every 375. In this province if you rake this same ratio, its to 560 memers of the public, so to get the ratio to the norm, we would get to the 4500.

LINK: Every community in the wcape is asking for extra policing, and its amazing what extra boots on the ground can achieve….like what has happened here in Boineheuwel.

VO: Bonteheuwel has over the years had some of the highest murder rates on the Cape Flats. Although crime fighting is the domain of police service, the CITY of Cape Town has flooded this suburb with a 100 of its own law enforcement officers from the 1st of July.

JP Smith: Moving beyond beyond being angry about what is bnot happening from NAT GOVT side, we are doing something as best we can ourselves and we have seen a significant improvement in the situation….my arguments to my colleagues in the city, they must replicate this initiative elsewhere

VO: The results from this operation have been surprising – and the city says it shows what extra policing can achieve.

Counsellor: its the first month for a very long time that we have had no gang related murder etc

VO: In the meantime, the future remains unclear for victims and witnesses like Roegshanda and her family. The court case where she testified has not been concluded and the private funds for their safe house are running out. But despite the hardship, she joined forces with other mothers this week…

Pascoe: I support the mom’s for justice, its all about the mothers that have lost their children. But also our police who have lost their lives trying to protect us.


Whilst socio economic upliftment and more police may reduce the crime on the cape flats, for now it’s the mothers and families who are digging in for the long haul.

Pascoe: As an activist it is dangerous, but I would rather be out there in the march in cape town defending our people, than dying as a coward.
